justification: PNPLA1 encodes a patatin-like phospholipase involved in omega-O-acylceramide synthesis in the epidermis, and biallelic variants cause autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis type 10 (and a comparable phenotype in golden retriever dogs). Immunodeficiency-centromeric instability-facial anomalies (ICF) syndrome is genetically explained by DNMT3B (ICF1), ZBTB24 (ICF2), CDCA7 (ICF3), and HELLS (ICF4), all involved in DNA methylation and pericentromeric heterochromatin maintenance. PNPLA1 has no known role in DNA methylation, centromeric heterochromatin, or immune function, and I am unaware of any report of PNPLA1 variants in ICF patients. Any co-mention would most likely be incidental (e.g., exome variant lists or gene panels), so the relationship is best classified as novel, with a small residual allowance for unknown functional or hypothesized links.

Bardet-Biedl syndrome 21 (BBS21) is caused by biallelic variants in C8orf37, a ciliary/photoreceptor gene, and the BBS gene family comprises BBSome and chaperonin-related ciliary genes. FCGR2B encodes the low-affinity inhibitory Fc-gamma receptor IIb, an immunoregulatory receptor on B cells and myeloid cells, best known for associations with systemic lupus erythematosus, immune thrombocytopenia, and malaria susceptibility. There is no known role for FCGR2B in ciliogenesis, retinal degeneration, or the BBSome, and no reported variants linking it to any BBS subtype. Any co-mention in the literature would be incidental (e.g., broad exome or GWAS datasets). A small residual probability is reserved for speculative immune/inflammatory modifier hypotheses in ciliopathy-related retinal degeneration.

Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease axonal type 2CC (CMT2CC) is a well-defined entity caused by heterozygous variants in NEFH (neurofilament heavy chain), with frameshift variants producing a toxic gain-of-function aggregation-prone protein. EDNRA, encoding the endothelin receptor type A, is associated with mandibulofacial dysostosis with alopecia (a neural crest–related craniofacial disorder) and with vascular traits such as coronary artery disease and migraine in GWAS; it has no reported role in inherited axonal neuropathies. Endothelin signaling has some relevance to neural crest and peripheral nerve/Schwann cell biology, which leaves a small possibility of loosely hypothesized biological connection, but there is no direct evidence relating EDNRA variants to CMT2CC. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel.

phenotype: autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2F
justification: Autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2F (LGMD R6) is definitively caused by biallelic variants in SGCD, encoding delta-sarcoglycan, with a well-established sarcoglycan complex disease mechanism. SCNN1A encodes the alpha subunit of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) and is associated with systemic pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 and CF-like/bronchiectasis phenotypes, not with muscular dystrophy. There is no reported human genetic evidence linking SCNN1A variants to LGMD2F, and ENaC is not a component of the dystrophin–glycoprotein/sarcoglycan complex of skeletal muscle. Any conceivable link would be indirect (ion channel/membrane physiology, or the unrelated skeletal muscle sodium channel SCN4A), leaving only a small allowance for a hypothesized biological rationale.

Acromelic frontonasal dysostosis is well established to be caused by a recurrent de novo missense variant (p.Arg1163Trp) in ZSWIM6, with sonic hedgehog pathway dysregulation as the proposed mechanism. ZNF81 is an X-linked zinc finger gene historically implicated in nonsyndromic X-linked intellectual disability (with later questions about pathogenicity), and it has no reported role in craniofacial or midline patterning disorders. I am not aware of any human genetic study, functional work, or animal model linking ZNF81 to frontonasal dysostosis phenotypes. The similarity is likely only superficial (both zinc-finger-containing genes), suggesting the pairing is incidental. A small residual probability is retained for obscure case reports or CNV studies involving Xp11.23 that might co-mention craniofacial features.

MHC class II deficiency (bare lymphocyte syndrome type II) complementation groups are caused by defects in the transcriptional regulators CIITA, RFXANK, RFX5, and RFXAP, with type 3 attributed to RFX5. SEC16B (SEC16L/RGPR) encodes an ER exit site scaffolding protein best known from GWAS for body mass index and obesity, with no reported role in MHC class II transactivation or in primary immunodeficiency. I am aware of no human genetic studies, functional immunology data, or animal models linking SEC16B variants to MHC class II expression defects. Any co-mention would be incidental, so the evidence overwhelmingly supports a Novel classification, with a small allowance for unrecognized secretory-pathway/antigen-presentation biology that could underpin a hypothesized link.

phenotype: short-rib thoracic dysplasia 11 with or without polydactyly
justification: Short-rib thoracic dysplasia 11 with or without polydactyly (SRTD11, OMIM 615633) is a well-defined ciliopathy caused by biallelic variants in WDR34, a dynein-2 intermediate chain gene; AGPAT5 is not among the recognized SRTD genes (which include IFT80, DYNC2H1, TTC21B, WDR19, NEK1, WDR35, EVC/EVC2, WDR60, IFT140, IFT172, CEP120, KIAA0586, etc.). AGPAT5 encodes 1-acylglycerol-3-phosphate O-acyltransferase 5, an enzyme in glycerophospholipid/triacylglycerol biosynthesis, with reported roles in lipid metabolism and metabolic traits rather than intraflagellar transport or skeletal ciliogenesis. I am unaware of any human genetic study reporting AGPAT5 variants in skeletal ciliopathy probands, nor of animal models linking it to thoracic hypoplasia or polydactyly. A small residual probability is assigned to Hypothesized because membrane lipid remodeling can indirectly influence ciliary membrane biology, and to Existing in case of an obscure or very recent case report I am not aware of.

Autosomal recessive Robinow syndrome type 2 (RRS2) is attributed to biallelic variants in NXN (nucleoredoxin), a WNT/PCP pathway regulator, while type 1 is caused by ROR2; both fit the WNT5A–ROR2–NXN signaling axis underlying Robinow syndrome. MRPS14 encodes a mitochondrial small ribosomal subunit protein and its reported human disease association is combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency 38 (COXPD38), presenting with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, growth restriction, dysmorphism, and lactic acidosis — a mitochondrial translation defect mechanistically unrelated to non-canonical WNT signaling. I am not aware of any clinical, functional, or model-organism evidence linking MRPS14 to Robinow syndrome. Any co-mention would most plausibly stem from overlapping nonspecific features such as growth delay or dysmorphism in variant databases rather than a genuine biological link. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with only small residual probability for a hypothesized connection.

phenotype: congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency
justification: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency is caused by mutations in CYP11B1 on chromosome 8q24, which is unlinked to the HLA region on 6p21. Historic linkage/haplotype studies explicitly tested HLA in 11β-OHD families and found no linkage, in contrast to 21-hydroxylase deficiency where CYP21A2 lies within the HLA class III region and shows strong HLA haplotype associations (e.g., HLA-B14/DR1 with nonclassic disease). Thus most HLA-DRB1 co-mentions with "congenital adrenal hyperplasia" pertain to the 21-hydroxylase form and are incidental to 11β-OHD, though this proximity/confusion in the literature and general HLA-adrenal autoimmunity biology gives a small residual weight to a hypothesized link. There is no credible human genetic evidence that HLA-DRB1 variation causes or modifies 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency, so the relationship is best classified as novel.

Common variable immunodeficiency type 3 (CVID3) is a well-defined OMIM entity attributed to biallelic loss-of-function variants in CD19, with a large body of replicated human evidence; WBP11 is not among the recognized CVID genes (which include ICOS, TNFRSF13B, CD19, TNFRSF13C, MS4A1, CD81, CR2, LRBA, PRKCD, NFKB1/2, IL21, IKZF1, IRF2BP2). WBP11 encodes a WW-domain-binding spliceosome-associated protein, and its documented human disease association is with congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT) and related developmental phenotypes, not B-cell immunodeficiency. I am unaware of any human genetic study, case report, or functional immunologic work linking WBP11 variants to hypogammaglobulinemia or impaired B-cell differentiation. A small residual probability is allotted to "hypothesized" because general spliceosomal/RNA-processing dysfunction can broadly affect lymphocyte development, providing a weak, nonspecific biological rationale. Overall, the pairing appears incidental, so the evidence best fits the Novel category.

Biallelic HELLS (LSH/SMARCA6) variants are established causes of ICF syndrome type 4 (immunodeficiency, centromeric instability, facial anomalies), not of spondylocostal dysostosis; the recognized SCD genes are DLL3, MESP2, LFNG, HES7, TBX6 and RIPPLY2, all in the Notch/somitogenesis pathway. I am unaware of any human proband or family with vertebral segmentation defects attributed to HELLS variants, which argues against Established or Existing. However, HELLS is a chromatin-remodeling ATPase required for DNA methylation, and Lsh-null mice show developmental defects including axial/vertebral skeletal abnormalities and derepression of Hox genes, providing a plausible but indirect biological rationale for a role in axial patterning. That murine/epigenetic evidence supports a moderate weighting for Hypothesized, while the absence of any human genetic link keeps most probability on Novel.

Silver-Russell syndrome 5 (SRS5) is, to my knowledge, attributed to HMGA2 variants (following SRS3/IGF2 and SRS4/PLAG1 within the IGF2–PLAG1–HMGA2 growth pathway), with no reported role for RAB32. RAB32 is a Rab GTPase involved in mitochondria-associated membranes, melanosome biogenesis, and immune/autophagy function; it has recently been implicated in Parkinson disease (p.Ser71Arg) and leprosy susceptibility, phenotypes unrelated to imprinting-related growth restriction. There is no known mechanistic or pathway connection between RAB32 and the IGF2/PLAG1/HMGA2 growth axis or 11p15/UPD7 imprinting mechanisms, and RAB32 (6q24.3) is not within a recognized SRS-associated imprinted interval, though its chromosomal neighborhood near the 6q24 imprinted region gives a very weak, incidental proximity argument. Accordingly, the evidence base is best described as absent, with only minimal probability of an obscure functional or single-case report I am unaware of.

phenotype: spinocerebellar ataxia, autosomal recessive, with axonal neuropathy 3
justification: Autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia with axonal neuropathy 3 (SCAN3, MIM 618387) is attributed to biallelic COX20 variants, and the related SCAN disorders are caused by TDP1 (SCAN1) and TDP2 (SCAN2); TTC21A is not among the recognized causal genes. TTC21A (IFT139-like) is instead reported in humans as a cause of asthenoteratozoospermia/sperm flagellar and head defects, with additional roles in intraflagellar transport, and its paralog TTC21B is linked to nephronophthisis/skeletal ciliopathies. Because ciliary/IFT dysfunction can occasionally involve cerebellar phenotypes (e.g., Joubert-spectrum ciliopathies), a limited biological rationale exists, justifying some weight for Hypothesized. However, I am unaware of any human genetic study reporting TTC21A variants in patients with recessive ataxia and axonal neuropathy, so the association is most consistent with Novel.

Immunodeficiency-102 is a distinct Mendelian immune disorder attributed to a specific gene (not MTHFR), and I am unaware of any clinical reports of MTHFR variants causing or segregating with this entity. MTHFR variants (e.g., c.665C>T/A1298C, severe MTHFR deficiency) are established causes of hyperhomocysteinemia/homocystinuria and neurologic/vascular disease, not a defined primary immunodeficiency phenotype. A plausible biological link exists because one-carbon/folate metabolism supports nucleotide synthesis and lymphocyte proliferation—illustrated by MTHFD1 deficiency causing combined immunodeficiency with megaloblastic anemia—so a hypothesized pathway relevance cannot be dismissed, and confusion with MTHFD1 may drive occasional co-mention. However, direct human genetic evidence tying MTHFR to immunodeficiency 102 appears absent, so the weight falls on Novel with secondary support for Hypothesized.

phenotype: myopathy, lactic acidosis, and sideroblastic anemia 1
justification: Myopathy, lactic acidosis, and sideroblastic anemia type 1 (MLASA1) is well established to be caused by biallelic PUS1 variants (with MLASA2 due to YARS2 and MLASA3 due to MT-ATP6); RNF220 is not among the recognized causal genes. RNF220 encodes a RING-type E3 ubiquitin ligase involved in Sonic hedgehog/Gli signaling and myelination, and biallelic RNF220 variants have been reported in humans in a distinct syndrome featuring hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, ataxia, spasticity and hearing loss — a phenotype unrelated to sideroblastic anemia or mitochondrial translation defects. I am unaware of any human genetic study linking RNF220 variants to sideroblastic anemia, lactic acidosis, or a MLASA-like mitochondrial myopathy. A small probability is reserved for a weak biological rationale (ubiquitin-mediated regulation of mitochondrial/heme pathways or an isolated case report) that I might not recall, but the pairing appears essentially incidental.

FKTN (fukutin) encodes a ribitol-phosphate transferase involved in alpha-dystroglycan O-mannosyl glycosylation; its established human disease associations are dystroglycanopathies (Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy, limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, Walker-Warburg syndrome) and dilated cardiomyopathy, all recessive. Autosomal dominant hypophosphatemic rickets is caused by gain-of-function variants in FGF23, with related phosphate-wasting disorders attributable to PHEX, DMP1, ENPP1, FAM20C, and SLC34A3. There is no known mechanistic or genetic link between fukutin-mediated glycosylation and renal phosphate handling or FGF23 signaling, and no reported ADHR families with FKTN variants. Any co-mention would be incidental (e.g., broad exome panels or muscle-weakness overlap in rickets). Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with a small allowance for speculative biology given that glycosylation influences FGF23 stability (though that involves GALNT3, not FKTN).

phenotype: familial isolated deficiency of vitamin E
justification: Familial isolated vitamin E deficiency (ataxia with vitamin E deficiency, AVED) is a well-characterized autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic mutations in TTPA, encoding the alpha-tocopherol transfer protein; no other gene has established causality. IFT54 (TRAF3IP1) encodes an intraflagellar transport-B complex component implicated in ciliopathies such as nephronophthisis-related syndromes, Senior-Løken/Bardet-Biedl-like phenotypes, and skeletal ciliopathies, with retinal degeneration as a recognized feature. Although retinal dystrophy can superficially overlap with the retinopathy seen in vitamin E deficiency, there is no mechanistic or genetic evidence linking IFT54 to tocopherol transport, absorption, or serum vitamin E levels. I am not aware of any human genetic study reporting IFT54 variants in patients with isolated vitamin E deficiency. A small probability is retained for hypothesized/existing in case of incidental co-mention in ataxia or retinal degeneration gene panels.

PIGC encodes a subunit of the GPI-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase complex, and biallelic PIGC variants have been reported in humans with an inherited GPI-anchor deficiency phenotype characterized by epilepsy, developmental delay and intellectual disability (e.g., Edvardson et al.), not with a B-cell defect or absent immunoglobulins. The established genetic causes of agammaglobulinemia are BTK, IGHM, IGLL1, CD79A/B, BLNK, PIK3R1, TCF3, SLC39A7, TOP2B and related B-cell developmental genes; PIGC is not among them. A weak, indirect biological rationale exists because GPI anchors are required for surface expression of several immune molecules (CD55, CD59, CD52, CD16b) and other PIG genes can produce immune-relevant phenotypes, which supports a modest allocation to "Hypothesized." However, I am not aware of any human proband or family in which PIGC variants segregate with agammaglobulinemia or profound hypogammaglobulinemia, so the bulk of probability lies with "Novel."

SLC52A2 encodes the riboflavin transporter RFVT2, and its pathogenic variants are well established as causing Brown–Vialetto–Van Laere syndrome type 2 / Fazio–Londe disease, a riboflavin transporter deficiency neuronopathy with sensorineural hearing loss and bulbar palsy. Guttmacher syndrome is a distinct autosomal dominant limb/genitourinary malformation disorder (postaxial polydactyly, hypoplastic thumbs, hypospadias, uterine anomalies) attributed to HOXA13 mutations and considered allelic with hand–foot–genital syndrome. There is no reported genetic, functional, or developmental-pathway link between SLC52A2 and the HOXA13-related limb malformation spectrum. Any co-mention would be incidental, e.g., in broad gene panel or database listings. Therefore the relationship is best classified as novel, with only a small allowance for unrecognized nomenclature overlap or speculative developmental riboflavin-deficiency arguments.

Familial hypercholesterolemia type 4 (OMIM 603813, autosomal recessive hypercholesterolemia) is attributed to LDLRAP1, with the other classic FH genes being LDLR, APOB, and PCSK9; VWA2 is not among the recognized causal or candidate genes for this disorder. VWA2 (AMACO) encodes a von Willebrand factor A domain–containing extracellular matrix–associated protein studied mainly in basement membrane biology and in colorectal cancer, with no established role in LDL receptor trafficking, clathrin adaptor function, or lipoprotein metabolism. I am not aware of human genetic studies, linkage results, or lipid GWAS signals implicating VWA2 in hypercholesterolemia, nor of relevant animal-model lipid phenotypes. Any co-mention is most likely incidental (e.g., exome/panel variant lists or large multi-gene screens), so the evidence base is best characterized as Novel, with small residual probability for an obscure association or biologically motivated hypothesis I may not recall.

RXYLT1 (formerly TMEM5) encodes a ribitol xylosyltransferase involved in the O-mannosyl glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan; its established human disease association is autosomal recessive muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy (MDDGA10/Walker-Warburg-like phenotype), not cholestatic liver disease. Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 8 is attributed to biallelic KIF12 variants (with other PFIC subtypes caused by ATP8B1, ABCB11, ABCB4, TJP2, NR1H4, MYO5B, USP53, ZFYVE19), and RXYLT1 is not among the recognized PFIC genes. There is no known mechanistic link between glycosyltransferase activity in the dystroglycan pathway and canalicular bile transport or hepatocyte tight-junction/ciliary biology underlying PFIC8. Although some congenital disorders of glycosylation can produce hepatic involvement, this is a generic association and does not constitute evidence for RXYLT1 in PFIC8, so a small residual weight is given to "hypothesized."

MCCC2 encodes the beta subunit of 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase, a biotin-dependent mitochondrial enzyme in leucine catabolism; its established human disease association is autosomal recessive 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency, an organic aciduria detected on newborn screening. Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 3 (VDDR3) is caused by gain-of-function variants in CYP3A4, leading to accelerated inactivation of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D; other VDDR subtypes involve CYP27B1, CYP2R1, VDR, and SEC23B/HNRNPC. There is no known mechanistic, pathway, or expression link between MCCC2 and vitamin D metabolism or rickets, and no reported patients with VDDR3 harboring MCCC2 variants. Any co-mention would likely arise incidentally from multigene metabolic panels or newborn screening literature. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with only a small allowance for unrecognized biotin/metabolic-bone speculation.

PNKP encodes polynucleotide kinase 3'-phosphatase, a DNA single- and double-strand break repair enzyme; biallelic variants cause microcephaly with seizures (MCSZ), ataxia with oculomotor apraxia type 4, and have been reported in a Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 2 phenotype — all neurological DNA-repair disorders. Hereditary systemic amyloidoses, including the numbered OMIM entries, are caused by variants in amyloidogenic secreted proteins such as TTR, APOA1, APOA2, LYZ, FGA, GSN, and CST3, none of which involve PNKP. There is no known mechanistic, pathway, or expression link between DNA-repair deficiency and hereditary amyloid fibril deposition, and I am unaware of any human genetic study or animal model connecting PNKP to systemic amyloidosis. Any co-mention in the literature would be incidental (e.g., large sequencing panels or 19q13 locus proximity). Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with only a small residual allowance for obscure functional speculation.

phenotype: early-onset progressive encephalopathy-hearing loss-pons hypoplasia-brain atrophy syndrome
justification: The disorder "early-onset progressive encephalopathy–hearing loss–pons hypoplasia–brain atrophy syndrome" corresponds to the phenotype described with biallelic TRAPPC12 variants (Milev et al., 2017), not TRPA1. TRPA1 in humans is established as the gene for autosomal dominant familial episodic pain syndrome 1 and has been studied in nociception, airway irritation, and inflammatory pain, with no reported role in a progressive infantile encephalopathy with pontine hypoplasia. A weak biological rationale exists because TRPA1 was once proposed as a candidate hair-cell mechanotransduction channel and is expressed in the inner ear and nervous system, which could loosely link it to hearing loss, but Trpa1-null mice have normal hearing and this is animal/in vitro evidence at best. The gene symbol similarity to TRAPPC12 ("TRAPP") may also cause incidental co-mention. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with a small allowance for a hypothesized biological connection.

ARC (arthrogryposis–renal dysfunction–cholestasis) syndrome is well established as a recessive disorder caused by biallelic variants in VPS33B and, less commonly, VIPAS39 (VIPAR), both involved in intracellular vesicle trafficking and apical membrane protein targeting. PDX1 is a pancreatic/duodenal homeobox transcription factor whose human variants cause pancreatic agenesis with neonatal diabetes and MODY4; its known phenotypic spectrum does not include arthrogryposis, renal tubular dysfunction, or cholestasis. There is no credible human genetic literature implicating PDX1 in ARC syndrome, and no compelling shared pathway or mouse-model evidence linking PDX1 to the ARC triad (though PDX1 has roles in hepatobiliary/duodenal development, which gives a very small biological rationale). Accordingly, the vast majority of probability falls in the Novel category, with a small allowance for tangential developmental/biliary biology arguments that could be framed as hypothesized.

CAV1 is not a recognized Mendelian cause of late-onset Parkinson disease and does not appear among established PD loci (SNCA, LRRK2, VPS35, GBA, etc.) or as a top hit in large PD GWAS meta-analyses. However, caveolin-1 has substantial mechanistic relevance: it organizes lipid rafts, modulates dopamine transporter trafficking, interacts with alpha-synuclein aggregation and membrane binding, influences autophagy, and is altered in aged and PD-affected brain and in rodent/cell models of dopaminergic degeneration — supporting a "Hypothesized" classification. Some small candidate-gene or expression studies in human tissue may report associations, so a modest probability is retained for "Existing," but these are not replicated in independent probands or families. There is essentially no basis for "Established," and "Novel" is unlikely given the well-documented biological plausibility.

phenotype: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
justification: ANAPC1 encodes the largest subunit of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome, a core cell-cycle ubiquitin ligase whose dysregulation (e.g., via CDC20, CDH1/FZR1, or APC/C substrates like cyclin B and securin) is broadly implicated in carcinogenesis, providing a plausible biological rationale for involvement in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. However, I am not aware of any replicated germline variant association, GWAS signal, or family-based evidence linking ANAPC1 variants specifically to HNSCC, so "Established" is very unlikely. Some points go to "Existing" because ANAPC1 could appear as a mutated or copy-number-altered gene in TCGA/exome sequencing surveys of HNSCC or in candidate-SNP studies, though such incidental somatic findings are typically not strong causal evidence. Most probability rests on "Hypothesized," reflecting pathway- and expression-level relevance without direct human genetic proof, with a substantial residual chance that the pairing is essentially unreported and therefore "Novel."

Developmental malformations–deafness–dystonia syndrome is classically attributed to a de novo ACTB variant (p.Arg183Trp; Procaccio et al.), and I am not aware of any human genetic study implicating PLEKHM2 in this entity. PLEKHM2 (SKIP) is best known as a kinesin-1 adaptor controlling lysosome and nuclear positioning, with its principal reported human disease association being biallelic loss-of-function causing dilated cardiomyopathy with left ventricular non-compaction in a consanguineous family. Its cytoskeletal/trafficking biology and 1p36 location give a weak, indirect rationale for developmental and neurological phenotypes, which supports a small allocation to Hypothesized. There is no replicated or even single credible human report linking PLEKHM2 variants to this specific syndrome, so most probability mass falls on Novel, with a modest hedge for an obscure case report or database annotation I may not recall.

PRDM6 is a well-characterized human disease gene, with heterozygous loss-of-function/missense variants established as a cause of nonsyndromic patent ductus arteriosus (PDA3), reflecting its role as a PR/SET-domain methyltransferase regulating smooth muscle differentiation. "Long-Olsen-Distelmaier syndrome" is an eponymous designation of the type OMIM applies to recently delineated Mendelian disorders named after the authors of the defining publication, which implies a specific gene assignment; if PRDM6 is that gene, the evidence would rest largely on a single index cohort report, favoring "Existing" or, if multiple independent probands/families were described, "Established." However, I cannot confirm from memory that PRDM6 is the gene underlying this particular eponym—the involved authors (Olsen, Distelmaier) are better known for mitochondrial/metabolic disease gene discovery, raising the real possibility that the eponym refers to a different gene entirely, in which case PRDM6 would be novel. Given this genuine uncertainty, I distribute points broadly, with slight weighting toward a true causal relationship because eponymous syndrome names are typically paired with a definitive gene, and PRDM6 has demonstrated human variant-disease causality in at least one other phenotype.

The OMIM entity "pulmonary hypertension, primary, 3" is attributed to KCNA5, not ISCA1, and I am unaware of ISCA1 variants being reported in PAH probands or families, so an Established designation is very unlikely. ISCA1's recognized human disease is multiple mitochondrial dysfunctions syndrome 5 (leukodystrophy, neurodevelopmental regression), in which pulmonary hypertension is not a consistent feature, although related iron–sulfur cluster assembly genes (NFU1, BOLA3, ISCU) are strongly tied to pulmonary hypertension in humans, giving some chance that a case report includes PH. The strongest support is mechanistic: Fe-S cluster biogenesis deficiency, hypoxia/miR-210–ISCU signaling, and mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming are well-documented drivers of pulmonary vascular remodeling, making a biologically plausible pathway link. Therefore most weight falls on Hypothesized, with residual probability on Existing (if a mutation-positive patient with PH exists) and on Novel (if co-mention is purely incidental).
